headline: October hike back to a coin flip.
standfirst: Tuesday took October from about 70% to about 50% priced in three hours: job openings fell to 7.079 million, a five-month low; the Conference Board's confidence index dropped to 81.9, the lowest since 2014; and John Williams said another hike this year is likely but there is 'no need for urgency'. The two-year fell 6bp to 4.87% while the thirty-year touched 5.621%, its highest since 2002, before closing near 5.57% — the first day since the hike on which the two ends of the curve disagreed. Stocks drifted, the S&P 500 down 0.17% to 7,670.84 and the Dow 0.26% to 51,349.92. Brent settled 2.6% lower at $102.59 and WTI 3.5% lower at $89.38 on recovering Saudi exports and a US strategic-reserve offer; the November Brent contract expires today about $7 above December. Overnight Australia's CPI printed 4.0% and the Aussie fell through 70 cents, China's PMIs went back above 50, the Nikkei rose 1.95% and the yen touched 156.38. It is quarter-end: ADP at 08:15 ET, PCE and final GDP at 08:30, three Fed speakers, Micron after the close.

bullets.title: Williams, JOLTS and a 2014 confidence low took October to 50%
bullets.text: August job openings fell 256,000 to 7.079 million, the lowest since March and below the 7.23 million expected, though July was revised up to 7.335 million; openings per unemployed worker slipped to 1.01 from 1.06, hires rose to 5.19 million and both quits and layoffs fell — softer demand, not firing. Consumer confidence fell 6.7 points to 81.9 against 89 expected, the lowest since 2014, with the present-situation index down 7.9 points, expectations down a third month, appraisals of current business conditions negative for the first time since September 2024, and write-ins about petrol prices at a record; for the first time in the question's four-year history more respondents called their finances bad than good. Then the Fed: Williams said another hike this year is likely if the economy meets expectations but there is 'no need for urgency' after September, and projected inflation reaching 2% only in 2028; Barr said further hikes may be necessary and policy needs recalibrating; Musalem said policy is still slightly accommodative. Futures pricing for 28 October fell to about 50% from about 70%; December remains the favoured date and roughly 75bp is priced for the cycle. Also on the tape: FHFA house prices +0.3%, Case-Shiller +0.1% and 1.9% on the year, the Dallas Fed services index back in contraction at −1.8.

bullets.title: Rates: the front end rallied, the long end set another two-decade high
bullets.text: The two-year touched a 52-week high of 4.96% in the morning and closed at 4.872%, down 5.8bp; the ten-year opened at 5.23%, hit 5.293% — the highest in 19 years — and closed at 5.232%, unchanged; the thirty-year rose for a sixth straight session, touching 5.621%, the highest since 2002, and closing near 5.567%, up 2bp. Two-tens steepened to about 36bp and the three-month-bill-to-ten-year gap is through 100bp for the first time this cycle. Demand at Tuesday's bill auctions was soft. Barclays now has the thirty-year reaching 6%; Wells Fargo puts the ten-year at 5.25–5.75% by the end of 2027; BNY notes the market still prices about 75bp of further tightening. The long Treasury ETF fell 0.50% and is down 12.47% over twelve months. In equities, the S&P 500 fell for a second day to 7,670.84, the Nasdaq 0.09% to 26,797.54 while the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.21%; Carnival jumped 13.4% on record revenue, Meta rose 3.24%, Apple fell 2.66%, Nvidia 0.72% and Tesla 1.29%. Utilities were the best sector at +1.17% as the front end rallied; energy fell 0.90%. The VIX closed at 16.04. Europe was mixed — DAX +0.28%, CAC −0.53%, FTSE −0.45% — and the euro-area sentiment index fell to 97.9.

bullets.title: Oil: Saudi exports recover, the US opens the reserve, and Brent's November contract expires today
bullets.text: November Brent settled at $102.59, down $2.69 or 2.6%, and WTI at $89.38, down $3.22 or 3.5%, as Saudi Arabia resumed loading at the Red Sea port of Yanbu via the restarted east–west pipeline, now carrying about 3.5 million barrels a day; ANZ has Saudi exports at 5.8 million barrels a day in September, the highest since February, Kpler has Hormuz flows at 13.2 million barrels a day or 77% of pre-war, and JPMorgan puts Middle East crude exports near 98% of pre-war levels. The US said it would offer up to 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and Trump is reportedly considering allowing sales of red-dyed diesel rather than an export ban, which Rystad called the most consequential near-term policy question for energy. Against that, Saudi August output was 6.24 million barrels a day, the lowest since 1990, Houthi attacks on Saudi facilities continue, Trump repeated he offered Iran 'nothing', and Qatar's foreign ministry said it is exchanging messages to find common ground with no reply yet delivered; Iran wants a seven-day ceasefire including Lebanon before reopening the strait, and Macquarie expects the standoff to run to the 3 November midterms. This morning November Brent is $103.30, December $96.51 and WTI $89.81; the November contract expires today, so the market map's Brent row already shows December and every front-month chart gaps down tomorrow. Brent is up about 14% in September, its best month since July; Murban traded near $120.

bullets.title: Overnight: Australia at 4.0%, China back above 50, the yen at 156.38
bullets.text: Australia's August CPI rose 4.0% year on year after 3.5%, a fraction under the 4.1% some surveys carried, with housing up 5.7%, transport 5.6% and fuel almost 15%; the trimmed mean held at 3.6% for a third month but the monthly core reading cooled to 0.2% against 0.3–0.4% expected. AUD/USD fell to a nine-week low of $0.6959, through 70 cents for the first time since early August, helped by Bullock's disclosure on Tuesday that the board had discussed holding before hiking; ANZ still expects a November hike to 4.85%, Oxford Economics does not, and CBA thinks the next big move in the currency is down. China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.1 and non-manufacturing to 50.2 against 49.3 expected, both back above 50 for the first time since June, with the composite at 50.7, the highest since December, construction at 50.3 and input prices at 60.8; the RatingDog measures came in at 52.1 and 51.6. Beijing added home-loan interest subsidies on Tuesday and markets close for Golden Week from tomorrow to 7 October. The Nikkei rose 1.95% to 66,755 on SoftBank and the chipmakers, Taiwan 1.12%, the ASX 1.02%; the Kospi was flat. USD/JPY touched 156.38, its strongest since 18 September, after Japan's top currency official repeated that the joint US–Japan warning was 'very clear' and July's BoJ minutes showed a debate on faster hikes. The dollar is up about 2.5% on the euro in September, its biggest monthly gain in 14 months, after the euro touched 1.1312 on Tuesday, its lowest since May 2025; the franc hit a 16-month low against the dollar and the kiwi its lowest since November. Gold rebounded 1.6% on Tuesday and is $4,210 this morning.

bullets.title: Today and the week: PCE and quarter-end, then ISM, then payrolls seen near 90,000
bullets.text: Wednesday: ADP at 08:15 ET seen 70,000 after 38,000; at 08:30 August PCE — core seen +0.3% on the month and 3.3–3.4% on the year after 3.3%, with a BEA methodology change that may trim the annual rate, headline +0.4% and 3.7% — alongside personal income +0.4%, spending +0.8% and final Q2 GDP at 1.5%; Chicago PMI at 09:45 seen 51.2 after 47.1; Cook at 15:25 ET, Goolsbee at 16:05, Kashkari at 18:00; Micron after the close; the Tankan at 19:50 seen 25 after 22; German HICP seen 3.1% and UK final GDP earlier in the day. Quarter-end rebalancing flows and the Brent expiry sit on top of all of it. Thursday: Swiss CPI seen 1.0%; ISM manufacturing seen 55.0 after 54.6 with prices paid 72.3; claims 200,000; Waller, Jefferson, Bowman, Cook and Williams; Lagarde; Nike after the close; Tokyo CPI; China shut. Friday: euro-area flash HICP seen 3.6% after 3.2% with core 2.5%; September payrolls with consensus between 84,000 and 100,000 after 162,000, Barclays at 50,000, unemployment seen 4.1%, earnings +0.3%. After Tuesday, payrolls is the print that decides whether October is a hike or a pause. Then Williams on 6 October, the FOMC minutes and ten-year auction on the 7th, the thirty-year and the ECB accounts on the 8th, the banks on the 13th, CPI and the Beige Book on the 14th.

calendar.event: ADP (September); PCE, income and final Q2 GDP 08:30
calendar.note: ADP seen 70,000 after 38,000. Core PCE seen 0.3% on the month and 3.3–3.4% on the year; the print the Fed named, on quarter-end, with October at 50%.
Seen 51.2 after 47.1. A regional read the day before ISM; the flash national PMI said 57.0.
Three speakers after the PCE print. Cook said Monday inflation pressure will persist for months; Kashkari is a 2026 voter closing out quarter-end day.

calendar.event: Micron Q4 after the close; November Brent expires
calendar.note: Earnings seen about $31 a share against $3 a year ago, with options implying a 9% move. From tomorrow every front-month Brent chart gaps about $7 lower; the map's Brent row already shows December.
Large manufacturers seen 25 after 22. With the BoJ debating faster hikes and the yen at 156, corporate confidence is a policy input.

calendar.event: ISM manufacturing (September); Nike after the close
calendar.note: Seen 55.0 after 54.6 with prices paid 72.3 after 71.1. The flash PMI said 57.0; a matching ISM keeps December live. China shuts for Golden Week.
Seen 3.6% after 3.2%, core 2.5%. The euro is at a 16-month low and Lagarde has promised measured steps; this is the print that decides whether 29 October is one.
Consensus 84,000–100,000 after 162,000, unemployment 4.1%, earnings +0.3%. With October at a coin flip after Tuesday, this print now decides it in both directions.

sessionNote: Quarter-end Wednesday opens with the curve disagreeing with itself: the two-year at 4.87% says the Fed can wait for December, the thirty-year at 5.57% says supply and term premium do not care. October is a coin flip, which means PCE at 08:30 ET matters again — a hot core print puts the hike back, a soft one is discounted as August data that does not know about September's oil. Stocks have drifted for two sessions inside the 7,650–7,690 gap; the S&P 500 held it on Tuesday. Oil has two prices today: November Brent near $103 expiring, December near $96.50 taking over, WTI $89.80 — quote the contract, not the ticker. Rebalancing flows into month- and quarter-end are largest in the last hour; the yen at 156.4 and the euro near 1.134 already carry some of them. In trading terms the session has one scheduled catalyst before the London close and none after it until Micron: 08:30 ET is the window, the Fed speakers from 15:25 ET are the echo, and anything that moves between them is flow.
watchOut: Reading today's tape as a verdict when half of it is calendar. It is the last day of September and of the third quarter: the S&P 500 is roughly flat on the month while long bonds have lost 5% and the dollar has gained 2.5% on the euro, so the rebalancing flow is out of equities and the dollar and into duration — a bond rally into the close today is a pension fund, not a change of view about the Fed. The second trap is the one Tuesday set up: October at 50% means every data point now swings the front end both ways, and PCE is the first. A core print of 0.3% is consensus, not a surprise; the reaction to a consensus print is positioning being squared, and it reverses. Size for a two-way 08:30 ET and a flow-driven last hour, and keep the Brent contract straight — the November expiry will print a $7 gap on Thursday's charts that no barrel traded through.

archive.headline: The ten-year closed at 5.24%. Nothing else mattered.
archive.summary: The ten-year closed at 5.236%, its highest since 2007, and the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to a ten-session low as Trump's rejection of Iran's Hormuz offer put Brent back above $107; Cook and Barkin talked rates higher, gold fell 3% to a seven-week low, and the RBA hiked to 4.60% overnight. The November Brent roll and Washington's reply to Tehran via Qatar were the day's traps.

archive.headline: Trump said no. Oil is back above $107.
archive.summary: Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz offer over the weekend and Brent recovered Friday's fall before New York opened; gold fell to its lowest since early August, the Kospi lost 2.5% and the dollar hit a two-month high. The front end eased with October's hike odds while the long end kept rising, into a week of PCE, ISM and payrolls.

archive.headline: The week the Treasury market stopped waiting for the Fed
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The ten-year went from 4.95% to 5.21% in a week on a 58.4 flash PMI, three auctions at two-decade highs and eight Fed speakers, and every Treasury from two years out cleared 5%. Equities held on Meta and AMD while the Dow fell for a fourth week, Brent round-tripped $100–$99–$106 on Iran, and October was 71% priced for a second hike.

archive.headline: A survey took the ten-year to 5.11%. An auction kept it there.
archive.summary: A flash composite PMI of 58.4, the highest since July 2021, took the ten-year up 14.6bp to 5.116% — its worst day since April 2025 — and a $70 billion five-year auction stopped at 5.033%, the highest since 2006. Barr said further hikes were likely needed and October went to 73% priced; every sector but energy fell and Brent rose back above $100.

archive.headline: The Fed said “we’ll see”. The two-year auction said 4.787%.
archive.summary: Treasury sold $69 billion of two-years at 4.787%, the highest stop since May 2024, on demand that held; Brent settled at $99.25 for its first close under $100 since 9 September; four Fed officials, none voting this year, all leaned toward more. The Nasdaq closed at a second straight record while financials fell 1.97%.

archive.headline: An App Store ranking moved a trillion dollars
archive.summary: Meta's Muse agent topped the US iPhone chart and the CPU complex repriced around it: Meta +11.43%, AMD +9.95% to a first $1 trillion close, Intel +12%, Arm +17%, and the Nasdaq to its first record since June. Crude fell to an eleven-day low on Hormuz shipping data and the ten-year came back under 5%, into a $69 billion two-year auction.

archive.headline: The war premium leaks out before the UN
archive.summary: Monday with no US data and a live diplomatic wire. Crude fell for a fourth session as traders priced a chance of US–Iran contact at the UN General Assembly and Saudi Arabia worked to restore its East–West pipeline, with the ten-year coming into the day at 5.01% after its first close above 5% since July 2007.
